Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose I should start with work, because that's really where it all kind of came to a head, you know? I'm a supervisor in retail, have been for a good long while, and communication is just... well, it's the whole job. You have to keep the floor moving and keep everyone on the same page. And instead of just saying who is on register one and who is in the back, my words just start... jumping. I'll start talking about the delivery trucks, and then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays, because Thursdays are when the big shipments come, but then my brain goes straight to the church grill—we had a barbecue there last summer, you see—and then I'm going on about my boss's tone of voice when he called me yesterday. And I look at my team, these people I supervise, and they just have these blank stares. People are looking at me like they absolutely cannot follow a single thing I'm saying. It's embarrassing, really, because I have a degree, I know how to run a store, but the words just pile up and spill out in all the wrong directions, and I can't seem to make them line up the way they used to, and it's just making everything at the store so much harder than it needs to be.

I can actually pinpoint it because six months ago, we were right in the middle of a massive seasonal transition. We were moving all the summer patio furniture and clearance items to the back wall to make room for the back-to-school pallets. It’s a huge undertaking, rearranging half the store overnight, and I was trying to explain the new planogram to my morning crew. I remember I was talking to Kevin—he’s one of my stock boys, good kid, hard worker, but you really have to spell things out for him step-by-step or he puts the wrong price tags on things—and my explanations just started coming out all jumbled. I knew exactly what I wanted him to do with the display bins, but the instructions were just getting completely tangled up on the way out of my mouth. 

And around that same time, I started doing these... these odd stops. Right out there on the sales floor. I’d be in the middle of directing a customer to the electronics department, or explaining the lunch break schedule to the cashiers, and I would just stop. Just freeze up, lose the thread entirely, and stand there in silence. The district manager even caught it once during a regional walk-through when I was trying to explain our inventory shrink numbers. I just stopped talking for a good ten or fifteen seconds, right by the register banks. He looked at me like I had two heads. 

So, yeah, it’s been a solid six months of these jumbled up explanations and weird pauses on the floor. I kept thinking it would just clear up once the back-to-school rush was over, you know, thinking it was just the stress of the reset, but then we went right into the Halloween sets, and then Thanksgiving, and it’s just stuck with me the whole time. It definitely didn't happen overnight, just sort of built up over the last half-year until it got to the point where I couldn't just brush it off as being tired anymore.

It's really just... it's just the words getting stuck, and the pacing in the battery aisle, and the freezing up with the clipboard. But inside? I'm exactly the same guy. Then there's the beep of the registers, the PA announcements, the sound of the pallet jacks rolling across the linoleum... it's a lot of noise. Sometimes, if I'm in the back room doing inventory, I might hear a thump and think someone dropped a box, but it's just the pipes, or the HVAC unit kicking on. Old building, you see. Built in the late 90s, I think. \n\nBut voices that aren't there? No. I hear my staff, I hear the customers complaining about the return policy—which, by the way, is printed right on the receipt, clear as day, but no one ever reads it. They just come up to the counter and expect you to bend the rules because they lost the tags. But that's real life, that's real people talking. I don't hear anything that nobody else hears. \n\nAnd as for strong beliefs... well, I believe in doing a good job. I believe in showing up on time, which is why I'm there at 7:00 AM sharp every day. I believe the district manager doesn't really understand the foot traffic patterns in our location, because he keeps pushing these endcap displays that just block the main aisle during the afternoon rush. I've told him this, of course. I sent a very detailed email about it last Tuesday, outlining the bottleneck it creates near the seasonal aisle. But nobody's telling me that's not true, they just ignore it because corporate mandates the floor plan. It's frustrating, but it's just business. Nobody is telling me I'm making things up or believing crazy things. It's really just my words, Doctor. Just the way they get all jumbled up when I'm trying to explain the shift changes or the break schedules. That's the only thing that's really out of sorts. Everything else is just the normal chaos of running a retail floor.\n\nDoctor: Around the time your words started getting jumbled, did you notice any other physical changes, like weakness, numbness, or drooping on one side of your face or body, or a sudden severe headache?\n\nPatient: Physical changes? No drooping at all. \n\nAnd a sudden, severe headache? Nothing sudden or severe. Nothing that makes me stop what I'm doing. It's really just the talking, Doctor. Just my brain not sending the right words to my mouth when I'm trying to run the morning huddle. The rest of my body is working exactly the same as it always has.\n\nDoctor: When you think back to when this word-jumbling first started, did it come on suddenly—like within a day or so—or has it been developing gradually over weeks or months?\n\nPatient: Suddenly? Oh, no. No, it wasn't like a light switch flipping, nothing like waking up one morning and suddenly not being able to get my sentences out. We were moving all the summer patio furniture and clearance items to the back wall to make room for the back-to-school pallets.
